summary: The C 350e is the plug-in hybrid grade of Mercedes-Benz Australia's C-Class sedan range, sold as a single specification at $99,418 before on-road costs — effectively the same list price as the mild-hybrid C 300 it comfortably out-accelerates — and it is the outgoing W206 model, with the updated C-Class due in Australia in the first half of 2027. Its 19.5kWh usable battery is good for 116km of WLTP electric range on the 18-inch rear-drive specification, and Australian reviewers are consistent that the calibration, the near-silent EV mode and the 11kW AC charging make it a genuine electric car for commuting. The criticisms are equally consistent: the battery takes the boot from 455 litres to 315, DC fast charging is a $1500 option rather than standard, and at $99,418 the car sits above both Luxury Car Tax thresholds and above the FBT cap with no plug-in hybrid exemption left to offset it.
pros: 116km of WLTP electric range from a 19.5kWh usable battery is the longest of any plug-in hybrid sedan in this dataset — well clear of the Audi A5 e-hybrid's 97km — and more than the heavier GLC 350e SUV manages on the same 230kW powertrain, so a typical Melbourne commute never starts the engine

It lists at $99,418 before on-road costs, $10 under the mild-hybrid C 300 petrol's $99,428, so the plug-in hardware costs nothing over a car it beats on outputs — 230kW/550Nm against the C 300's 190kW/400Nm, and 0-100km/h in 6.1 seconds

Charges properly for a plug-in hybrid: 11kW three-phase AC takes about two hours flat to full, and the optional 55kW DC fast charging ($1500) does 10-80 per cent in around 20 minutes, which almost no plug-in hybrid at this price offers at all
Braked towing is rated at 1800kg, unusually high for a plug-in hybrid sedan and only 600kg short of the GLC 350e SUV, so the battery has not cost it usefulness as a tow car
Mercedes-Benz Australia's five-year, unlimited-kilometre warranty is unconditional and is not tied to servicing inside the dealer network
cons: The battery costs the boot 140 litres: 315L against 455L in the petrol and mild-hybrid C-Class, which is less than the Audi A5's 331L and nowhere near a BMW i4's 470L, and Mercedes publishes no seats-folded figure for the plug-in saloon at all — the 40:20:40 rear seat does fold and load-through is possible, but you are buying a materially smaller boot than the badge implies

The 1.5L/100km combined label is meaningless once the battery is flat: the European WLTP battery-empty figure for the same rear-drive 230kW car is 6.6L/100km and Mercedes-Benz Australia quotes 7.6L/100km, on 95 RON premium either way, so a buyer who cannot charge at home is running a two-tonne petrol sedan and the whole case for the car collapses

At $99,418 it sits above both Luxury Car Tax thresholds — the ordinary $80,809 and the fuel-efficient $91,661 it qualifies for on its 1.5L/100km combined figure — and well above the $75,000 FBT cap, and since the FBT exemption for plug-in hybrids ended on 1 April 2025 there is no novated-lease advantage left to offset that

Servicing is expensive: Chasing Cars quotes $6890 for a five-year plan, and DC fast charging is a $1500 option rather than standard equipment, so the car that makes the strongest public-charging case among plug-in hybrids charges at 11kW unless you pay for it

It is a run-out model: the updated C-Class arrives in the first half of 2027, and Mercedes-Benz Australia publishes the current car's electric range as 104km under the NEDC-based ADR cycle rather than WLTP, with at least one Australian reviewer putting the real-world figure closer to 80km — the 116km WLTP figure recorded here comes from European homologation for the same 18-inch specification
